content: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is strongly recommended for adults and adolescents living with HIV who have a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³, based on moderate-certainty evidence. It may also be considered for those with a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³, though this is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. For individuals living with HIV who test positive for cryptococcal antigen during screening, a thorough evaluation for meningitis symptoms is essential. If feasible, a lumbar puncture should be performed to examine cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) using India ink or a CSF cryptococcal antigen assay to rule out active cryptococcal disease. Since India ink has low sensitivity, a negative result should be confirmed with a CSF cryptococcal antigen test. In settings where cryptococcal antigen screening is unavailable, fluconazole primary prophylaxis is recommended for those with a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³ and may be considered for those with a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³. For treating cryptococcal meningitis in people living with HIV, the preferred induction regimen includes amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg per day) and flucytosine (100 mg/kg per day, divided into four doses daily). Alternative induction regimens include two weeks of fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults or 12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents) combined with flucytosine or amphotericin B deoxycholate combined with fluconazole. Following the induction phase, fluconazole (400–800 mg daily for adults or 6–12 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents) is recommended for the consolidation phase over eight weeks. Maintenance therapy involves fluconazole (200 mg daily for adults or 6 mg/kg per day for children and adolescents). Routine use of adjunctive systemic corticosteroids during the induction phase of cryptococcal meningitis treatment is not recommended due to the risk of increased mortality. ART initiation should be delayed by 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment in individuals with cryptococcal meningitis to reduce mortality risk. For disseminated histoplasmosis in people living with HIV, diagnosis should involve detecting circulating Histoplasma antigens. Amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg daily for two weeks) is recommended for severe cases, while itraconazole (200 mg three times daily for three days, then 200 mg twice daily) is recommended for mild to moderate cases. Maintenance therapy with itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) for 12 months is advised, though shorter durations may be considered for clinically stable individuals with immune recovery on ART. ART should be initiated as soon as possible in individuals with disseminated histoplasmosis without central nervous system involvement. For those co-infected with tuberculosis (TB), HIV, and histoplasmosis, TB therapy should follow WHO guidelines. Children and adolescents living with HIV should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity daily, including muscleand bone-strengthening activities at least three days per week. Adults should aim for 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity weekly, with additional muscle-strengthening exercises on two or more days per week. Older adults should include multicomponent physical activities emphasizing balance and strength training to prevent falls. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for adults and children with severe or advanced HIV disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) or a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³. In high-prevalence settings for malaria or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be initiated regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage. It may be discontinued in clinically stable individuals on ART with immune recovery and viral suppression. Systematic TB screening is recommended for all individuals living with HIV at each health facility visit. Adults and adolescents should be screened using the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats). Those without symptoms should be offered TB preventive treatment. Children under 10 years should be screened for symptoms such as cough, fever, poor weight gain, or close contact with a TB patient. For latent TB infection, treatment options include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or three months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. In high TB transmission settings, daily isoniazid preventive therapy for 36 months is recommended for individuals living with HIV, regardless of ART status or immune suppression. Routine testing for chronic hepatitis B (HBV) infection is recommended in settings with ≥2% or ≥5% HBsAg seroprevalence. Pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and HBsAg early in pregnancy. All infants should receive their first dose of the HBV vaccine within 24 hours of birth. Focused testing for hepatitis C (HCV) infection is recommended for populations most affected by HCV, such as people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons, and those with high-risk behaviors. Testing should include serological assays for HCV antibodies, with linkage to care and treatment services. Preventing mother-to-child transmission of HBV involves testing all pregnant women for HIV, syphilis, and HBsAg early in pregnancy and ensuring timely HBV vaccination for newborns.
